doc: Decode speed prompts of about 1.3k tokens (SPD-183): a system prompt and two workloads, code and prose, each sent as the user turn after the nonce line. The text is versioned: any change to it is a new file with a new version. token_counts: the 27B's tokenizer and chat template, thinking off, with a 32-hex nonce (8 nonces; min and max).
system: You are a senior engineer on a small infrastructure team. Work carefully and give a complete, technically precise answer. Follow the brief exactly; when the brief and your habits disagree, the brief wins. Do not mention benchmarking or the request nonce.

workloads.code:
Implement a compact, production-quality Go package for one concurrency-safe token-bucket rate limiter. Include an injectable clock, AllowN, constructor validation, and table-driven tests using a fake clock. Return only one implementation code block and one test code block, each with its filename, and no prose. Keep the complete answer below 1,100 words.

Context. The package is called ratelimit and lives at internal/ratelimit in a service that fronts a batch inference queue. Three callers share one limiter: the HTTP handler that admits new jobs, a background retry loop, and an admin endpoint that drains the queue. They call it from many goroutines at once, so every exported method must be safe for concurrent use without the caller holding any lock. The service runs on Go 1.22, uses only the standard library, and is built with -race in CI; the race detector must stay quiet under the tests you write.

The bucket. A limiter has a refill rate r in tokens per second and a burst b, the bucket's capacity. It starts full. Tokens accrue continuously: after an idle time d the bucket holds min(b, tokens + r*d). Keep the token count as a float64 so that fractional refill is not lost between calls, and compute refill lazily from the clock on each call instead of running a ticker or a goroutine. Taking n tokens succeeds only when at least n are present; a call that fails must leave the bucket exactly as it found it, apart from the refill that was due. A request for zero tokens always succeeds and changes nothing. A request for more than the burst can never succeed and must say so without waiting.

The clock. Define a small Clock interface with one method, Now() time.Time, a realClock type that wraps time.Now, and an option that lets tests pass their own clock. The limiter must read the time exactly once per call and never call time.Now directly. If the clock goes backwards (a fake clock set earlier, or a wall-clock jump), treat the elapsed time as zero rather than draining or overfilling the bucket.

The API. New(rate float64, burst int, opts ...Option) (*Limiter, error). Allow() bool is AllowN(1). AllowN(n int) bool takes n tokens if they are present and reports whether it did. Tokens() float64 reports the current level after refill, for metrics. Reserve-style waiting is out of scope: no Wait, no context, no channels. Options are functional options; the only one needed is WithClock(Clock).

Validation. New returns an error, and no limiter, when the rate is not a finite number greater than zero, when the burst is less than one, or when a nil clock is passed to WithClock. Use errors that callers can test with errors.Is: declare ErrInvalidRate and ErrInvalidBurst as package variables and wrap them with the offending value in the message. A negative n passed to AllowN is a programming error; return false and leave the bucket unchanged rather than panicking.

Style. Keep the implementation under about 120 lines. Use a sync.Mutex, not atomics, and keep the critical section to the refill arithmetic and the take. Document every exported identifier with a sentence that starts with its name. Name the unexported refill helper advance and give it the current time as a parameter so it can be reasoned about without the clock. No global state, no init functions, no logging.

Tests. Write the tests in package ratelimit_test against the exported API only, with a fakeClock type that holds a time.Time behind its own mutex and has an Advance(d time.Duration) method. Cover, as rows of one or more tables: construction errors for a zero, negative, NaN and infinite rate, a zero and negative burst, and a nil clock; a fresh limiter allowing exactly burst single requests and then refusing one; refill after half a second at a rate of two tokens per second giving back exactly one token; refill capping at the burst after a long idle period; AllowN with n equal to the burst, n above the burst, n of zero and a negative n; a failed AllowN leaving Tokens unchanged; a clock that moves backwards; and fractional refill accumulating across several short advances until a whole token is available. Add one concurrency test that starts 32 goroutines calling Allow on a limiter with a burst of 100 and no refill (the fake clock never advances) and checks that exactly 100 calls succeed in total. Use t.Run with a descriptive name for every table row, compare floats with a small tolerance helper, and keep each test function short.

Repository conventions. Errors are wrapped with fmt.Errorf and the %w verb, never compared by string. Exported constructors return a pointer and an error, and never a half-built value. Durations in tests are written as multiples of time.Millisecond or time.Second, not as raw integers. Table rows are structs with a name field first, and the loop variable is copied before t.Run on older toolchains, though this module already builds with 1.22 semantics. Floating-point tolerance in tests is 1e-9 unless a row needs a looser bound, and the helper that checks it should report both values on failure. The reviewers on this team reject code that sleeps in tests, that uses time.After in production paths, or that exports a field only so a test can read it. Keep imports grouped with the standard library first, and do not add a doc.go file for a package this small. The package comment goes above the package clause in the implementation file.
workloads.prose:
Write a thoughtful internal engineering memo of roughly 700 words. A small team must decide whether to buy more local AI hardware or improve utilisation of what it owns. Weave cost, latency, reliability, opportunity cost, and reversibility into natural prose. Make a clear recommendation, acknowledge uncertainty, and avoid lists.

Background for the memo. The team is six engineers at a mid-sized logistics company. Eighteen months ago it bought two workstation-class inference boxes, each with 128 GB of unified memory, to run an open-weight 27-billion-parameter model locally instead of sending shipment documents to a hosted API. The boxes serve three internal tools: a document extractor that reads customs forms and invoices overnight, a chat assistant that dispatchers use during the day, and a code-review helper that the platform team runs on every merge request. Legal asked for the move off the hosted API because the documents contain customer addresses and contract prices, and that requirement has not changed.

Usage today. The dashboard shows the two boxes busy about 31 percent of the hours in a month. The overnight extractor keeps both of them near full load from about one to five in the morning. During working hours the chat assistant peaks at eleven and again at three, when up to fourteen dispatchers ask questions at once; at those peaks the median time to the first word of an answer rises from under one second to about six seconds, and dispatchers have started to complain. The code-review helper runs in bursts after lunch and is the one tool nobody would miss for an hour. Each box serves one model with a single request queue; there is no batching across requests, no prompt caching, and no priority between the three tools, so a long code review can sit in front of a dispatcher's question.

The proposal on the table. Procurement has a quote for two more boxes of the same type at 4,200 euros each, plus about 600 euros a year in power and rack space, with delivery in five weeks. The finance lead wants a decision before the budget closes at the end of the month, and notes that hardware bought now is written off over three years and cannot easily be resold at a good price. One engineer argues that four boxes would let the team split the tools so that the dispatchers never wait behind anything else.

The alternative. Two engineers spent a week last quarter testing a newer serving engine on one box. With continuous batching and a prefix cache for the long system prompt the chat assistant uses, the same box answered eight concurrent chat requests with a median first-word time of 1.4 seconds, and total throughput rose about three times. They also prototyped a priority rule that lets chat requests overtake code reviews. The work was never finished: the new engine needs a different quantised model file, the extractor's output changed slightly on about two percent of documents in a spot check, and nobody has had time to validate that difference or to write the runbook. Finishing it is estimated at three to five engineer-weeks, which would come out of the warehouse-scanner project that the operations director has been promised for next quarter.

Risks people raised. The boxes have been reliable, with one unplanned outage in eighteen months, caused by a full disk. With only two machines, one failure halves capacity and the overnight run would finish late; a third box would remove that risk. The newer engine is younger software with a smaller community, and the team would be among its heavier users. If the company later moves the chat assistant to a hosted model with a data-processing agreement, which legal has said might be acceptable for chat but not for documents, extra boxes would sit mostly idle, while software improvements would still help the extractor. Usage has grown about eight percent a month since spring, mostly from the chat assistant.

Numbers from finance. Over three years the two extra boxes cost about 10,200 euros including power, against roughly 1,500 euros a month that the hosted API cost before the move, so the original purchase paid for itself within the first year. An engineer-week is costed internally at about 2,400 euros, which puts the software route at 7,200 to 12,000 euros in time, though that money is not a cash outlay and does not touch the hardware budget. If the budget is not used this month, the hardware line does not roll over into next year.

What people said in the meeting. The dispatch lead said the six-second waits are tolerable for now but would not be if the planned second shift starts using the assistant in the spring, which could roughly double peak demand. The platform lead said the code-review helper could move to the overnight window if needed, since nobody reads its comments before the next morning anyway. The operations director said the warehouse-scanner project slipping by a month would be awkward but not serious, while slipping by a quarter would cost goodwill with two depots that were promised it. One of the engineers who ran the batching test said the two percent difference in extracted fields came mostly from rounding in unit prices and needs a proper check, not a guess, before anyone trusts it. The head of engineering asked, half joking, whether the honest answer was both, and nobody replied. The finance lead added that a smaller order of one box is also possible at the same unit price, and that the vendor would hold the quote until the budget closes. Nobody has yet asked the dispatchers which of their questions could wait a few seconds and which could not, and the logs keep only the times, not the questions, so that is not known either.

What the memo should do. Address it to the head of engineering, who will decide, and to the finance lead. Explain the trade-off in plain language that a non-specialist can follow, use the numbers above where they help, say what you would do and why, name what would change your mind, and suggest how to keep the decision reversible. Write it as connected paragraphs with a short title line, in the voice of the team's senior engineer.
